# Resolution Adaptation

Also called: Adaptive Resolution, Dynamic Resolution, Resolution Scaling

## Overview
Resolution Adaptation modulates spatial sampling density or grid resolution during volume rendering to balance visual fidelity against computational cost [G]. It solves fixed-performance bottlenecks by dynamically adjusting the rendering budget based on metrics like frame time, training iteration, or spatial complexity [G]. Unlike static resolution methods, this family continuously or periodically adapts sampling rates, distinguishing it from siblings like [Random Pixel Subsampling](1668-random-pixel-subsampling.md) (alters ray count) and [Two-stage NeRF Rendering](925-two-stage-nerf-rendering.md) (coarse-to-fine refinement) [G].

## Shared principles
Builds on the parent's shared principles [Adaptive Sampling and Resolution](1412-adaptive-sampling-and-resolution.md).

## Subtopics

### [Level-of-detail (LOD) methods](1007-level-of-detail-lod-methods.md)
Maintains interactive frame rates by dynamically changing rendering resolution to match computational budget. Sets itself apart by adapting sampling density or geometric approximation in real-time based on performance metrics, rather than using static pre-computed hierarchies. Choose when interactive manipulation requires trading visual fidelity for speed.

### [Dynamic Volume Resolution & Alpha Mask Update](2539-dynamic-volume-resolution-alpha-mask-update.md)
Dynamically adjusts voxel grid resolution and active spatial bounding box during neural volume training. Sets itself apart by coupling resolution upscaling with alpha mask updates to prune empty background space. Choose when training efficiency and memory usage are bottlenecks.

### [Dynamic Resolution Adaptation](2683-dynamic-resolution-adaptation.md)
Runtime technique adjusting render viewport reduction factor based on previous frame time and allocated budget to maintain target frame rate. Sets itself apart by continuously shifting resolution levels based on frame time gradients rather than fixed blending factors. Choose when parametric changes cause performance instability or cybersickness.

### [Mixed-Resolution Multi-Volume Rendering](3193-mixed-resolution-multi-volume-rendering.md)
Renders different channels of a multi-volume dataset at different resolution levels to save memory and reduce samples. Sets itself apart by operating on a per-channel basis within a single ray traversal, rather than switching dataset resolution globally. Choose when channels have varying frequency content or visual importance.

### [Volume Level-of-Detail (LOD) Rendering](4614-volume-level-of-detail-lod-rendering.md)
Maximizes image quality within frame rate and hardware constraints by adaptively modifying rendered octree cells. Sets itself apart by maintaining an active cut of the octree that splits/merges nodes every frame, explicitly managing hierarchical non-leaf nodes rather than just alpha masks or global scales. Choose when maintaining interactivity for large hierarchical datasets.

### [Focus and Context Multiresolution Rendering](8163-focus-and-context-multiresolution-rendering.md)
Balances processing between a high-detail focus region and a lower-detail context region to improve interactivity. Sets itself apart by decomposing rendering into two passes with distinct parameters, explicitly trading seamless integration for speed. Choose when hardware resources are limited and time-critical applications require prioritized detail.

### [Multiresolution Atlas Buffer (MAB)](8219-multiresolution-atlas-buffer-mab.md)
Acceleration wrapper for DVR in VR that reduces ray density based on peripheral vision and HMD lens distortion, reconstructing full resolution via compositing. Sets itself apart by operating as a bracket around existing raycasters (modifying ray construction and compositing) rather than modifying traversal or volume resolution, and not requiring eye-tracking hardware. Choose for VR applications needing high refresh rates without eye-tracking.

#### Mixed Resolution Scene Rendering
Combines full-resolution scene elements with low-resolution high-density volume data by rendering the volume to off-screen targets and projecting them onto a quad [S1]. Setup involves two off-screen cameras (one per eye) updating each frame, two low-resolution render targets (e.g., 200x200), and a quad moving in front of the user [S1]. Each frame: draw low-resolution render targets for each eye (volume data, expensive shaders), draw the scene normally at full resolution (meshes, UI), and draw the quad projecting the low-res renders onto it [S1].

#### Resolution and Frame Splitting
High-end systems reduce resolution to 1/2x1/2 [S2, unofficial]. Mid/Low-end systems use frame splitting (similar to RDR2), simplified for clouds not intersecting other objects [S2, unofficial].

## Background
Resolution adaptation in volume rendering originated from the need to handle large datasets interactively [G]. Early implementations focused on Level-of-Detail (LOD) techniques for unstructured grids and octrees to maintain frame rates during viewpoint changes [1007-level-of-detail-lod-methods.md][4614-volume-level-of-detail-lod-rendering.md]. With the advent of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and neural volumes, the concept evolved into dynamic resolution updates during training to optimize memory and convergence [2539-dynamic-volume-resolution-alpha-mask-update.md]. In real-time graphics and VR, techniques like Dynamic Resolution Adaptation and Multiresolution Atlas Buffers were developed to manage strict frame time budgets and leverage human visual system properties [2683-dynamic-resolution-adaptation.md][8219-multiresolution-atlas-buffer-mab.md].
